transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess the main thing is… since I stopped working, I don’t seem to know how to slow down. I thought retirement, or being out of work, whatever you want to call it at my age, would mean I’d finally sit still a little, maybe take it easy. But instead I’m up and moving around all day, going from one little job to the next.

It’s like I still have a crew waiting on me or something, like there’s always another task that has to be done right now. I’ll finish one thing and then I’m already looking for the next thing to fix or clean up or move around. I don’t really settle. It’s not that the jobs are always important either — sometimes it’s just little stuff — but I keep going like I’m still on the clock.

So that’s why I’m here. I’m not working anymore, but my body and my head don’t seem to have gotten that message.
Do you feel like you have to do these tasks, or is it more that you just can't seem to stop yourself from looking for the next thing to do?

It’s more that I can’t seem to stop looking for the next thing, I think. I don’t know that I’d say I feel forced exactly, like somebody’s making me do it, but once I’m up and going, my head just starts scanning for what’s next.

I’ll finish one little job, and instead of sitting down, I’m already noticing something else — a tool out of place, something that needs wiping down, something in the garage I could straighten. And then I’m off doing that. It’s like I’m still in work mode, like there’s a crew waiting on me and I’ve got to keep things moving, even though there isn’t anybody waiting and none of it is that urgent.

So yeah, it’s not so much “I have to” in a clear way. It’s more I just don’t naturally stop.
Do you ever find yourself thinking about these tasks or chores even when you're not actively doing them?

Yeah, I do, though sometimes it’s not exactly the chore itself so much as something around it pulling my head away. Like if I’m trying to sit down and do something quiet — I’ve been messing around with painting a little, or I’ll try to plan out a story idea in my head — and then I hear a truck go by outside, my mind just jumps right over there. I’ll start wondering who that is, whether it’s a delivery, whether I left something out by the driveway, and then I’ve lost the thread of what I was doing.

Same with the garden. I can be in the middle of thinking through something, and suddenly I remember, oh, I should check that one plant, or maybe I ought to move that hose, or there was something I meant to look at out there. And once that thought comes in, it’s like the thing I was trying to focus on just sort of disappears. I’ll sit there with the paintbrush or the paper in front of me and think, now where was I?

So yes, my mind does go off to those things, even when I’m not actually doing them. It doesn’t always feel like I’m deliberately choosing to think about them — it’s more like some little noise or idea hooks me, and then I’m over there instead of where I meant to be.
Do you feel anxious or unhappy when you're not able to keep moving from one task to another?

I don’t know that I’d call it anxious exactly, or unhappy in the way you might mean. It’s more like I get… unsettled, I guess. Like if I’m not moving from one thing to the next, something feels off, like I’m wasting time or I’m supposed to be doing something.

Since I stopped working, that’s been the strange part. I thought I’d slow down, but I don’t. I’m still up all day, going from one little job to another, almost like I’ve still got people depending on me to keep things running. There’s no crew waiting on me anymore, nobody asking me to get anything done, but my body acts like there is.

So if I try to just sit there, I don’t always feel bad exactly, but I don’t stay there long. I start looking around, noticing something that could be fixed or cleaned or moved, and then I’m back up again. It’s like I don’t know how to just stop.
Do you find yourself repeating certain tasks or behaviors over and over?

I’m not sure I’d say I repeat the same thing over and over in a set way. Not like I have to touch something a certain number of times or keep checking the same lock or anything like that — at least, I haven’t really noticed that.

I do circle back to things sometimes, but it feels more like I forgot where I left off or I notice something again and think, “Oh, I should deal with that,” not like a ritual. Like I might tidy an area, then later see another thing out of place and end up back over there, but it’s not the exact same behavior in my mind.

So… I guess no, not repeating in a particular pattern. More just moving around and getting pulled into things as they come up.
Do you have thoughts that keep coming back to you, even when you try to think about something else?

Yes, that happens. It’s not always a big important thought, either. It can be something small, but once it pops in, it keeps tugging at me.

Like if I’m trying to paint — and I’m not saying I’m any good at it, it’s just something I’ll sit down with — I’ll be trying to think about the color or what I was going to do next, and then I hear a truck outside. Right away my mind goes to that. I start wondering, “Is that stopping here? Is that a delivery? Did I leave something out there?” And even if I tell myself, no, just keep painting, I’ve already lost the place I was in. Then I’m sitting there looking at the brush like I don’t quite remember what I meant to do.

Or with story ideas, same sort of thing. I’ll be trying to plan something out in my head, and then I’ll suddenly think of the garden — maybe there was a plant I meant to check, or something I was going to move — and that thought keeps coming back until I either go look or I completely lose track of the story idea.

So yes, thoughts do come back and pull me off what I’m trying to think about. It’s not like I want them to; they just sort of jump in and take over.
Do you feel like you're doing these tasks to prevent something bad from happening?

No, I don’t think so. At least, not in the sense of, “If I don’t do this, something terrible will happen.” It doesn’t feel like that.

It’s more like… I notice something, and then it starts bothering me that it’s unfinished or sitting there. Like if I see something out of place, I don’t usually think, “Oh, if I don’t move that, there’ll be a disaster.” It’s just there in my head, kind of poking at me, and then I feel like I may as well deal with it. Or I worry I’ll forget about it if I don’t do it right then.

So I wouldn’t say I’m trying to prevent something bad. It’s more that I get pulled into doing it because it’s in front of me or because the thought won’t leave me alone.
Do you feel distressed when these thoughts or urges to do tasks interrupt what you're trying to focus on?

Yes, I do get distressed, though maybe “distressed” sounds a little stronger than how it always is. It’s more like I get frustrated and sort of thrown off, because I’ll be trying to stay with one thing and then my mind just jumps tracks.

Like if I’m painting, I might actually be settled for a minute, thinking about what color I’m using or where I was going to put the next bit, and then I hear a truck outside. It doesn’t even have to be anything important. Just that sound, and suddenly my head is over there — wondering what it is, whether it’s stopping nearby, whether I need to look. And then when I try to come back, I’m staring at what I was doing like I lost the thread.

Same with planning a story. I’ll be turning an idea over in my head, and then something about the garden pops up — a plant I meant to check or something I noticed earlier — and my mind goes right there instead. Then I’m annoyed because the story thought is gone, or at least it’s harder to get back.

So, yes, it bothers me. Not panic or anything like that, but it’s upsetting in the sense that I can’t just keep hold of what I meant to focus on.
Are you having trouble maintaining relationships or participating in social activities because of your need to constantly be doing tasks?

Well… I wouldn’t say I’m losing relationships over it, exactly, but it does get in the way some. Since I stopped working, I just don’t seem to know how to slow down. I’m up and moving from one little job to the next all day, almost like I still have a crew waiting on me or like there’s some schedule I’m supposed to be keeping.

So if there’s something social going on, I might have a hard time just settling into it. My mind will go to, “I should finish that first,” or “Let me just take care of one more thing,” and then one thing turns into another. It’s not that I don’t want to be around people. It’s more that I’m always half-pulled toward doing something, even small stuff.

I don’t think it’s ruined anything, but I can see how it makes me less available than I should be. I have trouble just sitting and being there without feeling like I ought to be up doing some task.
Do you feel like your need to constantly be doing tasks is affecting your overall quality of life?

Yes… I think it is, more than I like to admit. It’s not like my whole life is falling apart, but it’s enough that other people have had to start working around me, and that doesn’t feel good.

My wife, for one, has pretty much taken over keeping the calendar, because if it’s left to me, I’ll either forget to look at it or I’ll get caught up doing some little task and miss the bigger thing I was supposed to do. She also checks behind me more than she used to, which I know is probably frustrating for her. I don’t think she means it in a harsh way, but I can tell it’s become a role she’s had to take on.

And outside the house, I’ve had to apologize more than once to people at the community center and the garden group because I said I’d do something or show up for something, and then I let them down. Usually it’s not because I don’t care. It’s because I get wrapped up in one thing after another, or I lose track, and then by the time I realize, I’m embarrassed and trying to explain myself.

So yes, I’d say it affects my quality of life. Maybe mildly, compared to some people, but it affects my confidence. I don’t like feeling like my wife has to manage me or like other people can’t count on me.
Do you feel like your inability to stop doing tasks and your constant need to be active is significantly interfering with your daily life and causing you a lot of distress?

Yes… I mean, I don’t know if I’d say “a lot” of distress every minute, but it is interfering, yes. What really brings me in is that since I stopped working, I can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and moving from one little job to the next all day, like I still have a crew waiting on me or some deadline hanging over me.

It’s strange, because there isn’t always anything urgent. I’ll just see something that could be done, and then I’m doing it, and then that leads to another thing. Before I know it, the day’s gone and I don’t feel like I ever really settled. It’s not relaxing, exactly. It feels like my body and my mind are still in work mode, even though I’m not working anymore.

So yes, it does affect my daily life. I don’t feel like I can just stop and be still the way I probably should be able to. It wears on me.
Are you finding it difficult to fulfill responsibilities or maintain a daily routine due to your constant need to be active and do tasks?

Yes, it does make it harder, especially with the day-to-day responsibilities. I don’t mean that I can’t do anything at all, but things don’t stay organized if it’s just left to me.

My wife has had to take over keeping the calendar, for example. She’ll remind me where I’m supposed to be or what we said we’d do, because I’ll get busy with some task and lose track of the bigger picture. And she checks behind me more now, too — not in a mean way, but because if she doesn’t, something may slip through. I don’t like that. It makes me feel like she has to manage me.

And outside the house, it’s happened with the community center and the garden group. I’ve had to apologize more than once because I said I’d be there or said I’d take care of something, and then I let people down. Usually I’m not sitting around doing nothing — I’m doing something — but it’s the wrong thing, or I get caught up in one thing after another and don’t follow through on what I was actually responsible for.

So yes, I’d say it interferes with keeping a routine and fulfilling responsibilities. Maybe not in a dramatic way every day, but enough that other people notice and have had to adjust around me.
Are there any areas of your life where you feel like your constant need to be active and do tasks is causing problems for you?

Yes, there are a couple areas where it’s caused problems, and I guess I keep circling back to the same ones because they’re the ones that bother me the most.

At home, my wife has really had to take over the calendar and the keeping-track-of-things part of our life. If there’s an appointment, or something we said we’d go to, or some responsibility we agreed to, she’s usually the one making sure it’s written down and that I actually remember it. And it’s not just reminders — she checks behind me sometimes, too, because I’ll say I handled something, but then maybe I got pulled into another task and didn’t finish the first one properly. I don’t like putting that on her. It makes me feel like she has to supervise me, and that’s not a great feeling at my age.

And then with things outside the house, like the community center and the garden group, I’ve had to apologize more than once because I let people down. I’ll tell someone I’ll be there, or I’ll say I’ll take care of something, and then I get busy doing other stuff and somehow the thing I promised gets missed. It’s embarrassing, because I do care. I’m not trying to be unreliable. But from their side, I imagine it just looks like I didn’t follow through.

So yes, mostly it’s causing problems in my marriage and in those volunteer or community commitments — not huge disasters, maybe, but enough that people have had to adjust around me.

Are you finding that your difficulty in stopping tasks and constant need to be active is significantly impacting your ability to engage in activities you enjoy or to spend quality time with family and friends?

Yes, I think it does, at least in the sense that I don’t really settle into things the way I used to imagine I would after retiring. What brings me in, really, is that since I stopped working, I can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and moving from one little job to the next all day, almost like I still have a crew waiting on me or some deadline I’m supposed to meet.

So if I’m supposed to just sit with family, or spend time with someone, or enjoy something quietly, it’s hard for me to stay there mentally and physically. I’ll notice something that “needs” doing, or I’ll think of some small task, and then I’m up. And then that task leads to another one. It’s not always that I’m choosing chores over people on purpose — it’s more like I get pulled along by whatever is in front of me.

I don’t want to make it sound like I never enjoy anything or never spend time with anyone, because that wouldn’t be fair. But the constant moving, the feeling like I should be doing the next thing, it does get in the way of just being present. That’s probably the part that bothers me most.
Are you feeling overwhelmed or stressed by your inability to stop doing tasks and constant need to be active?

Yes, I do feel stressed by it. Not every minute like I’m panicking or anything, but it wears on me. What brings me in, really, is that since I stopped working, I can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and moving from one little job to the next all day, like I still have a crew waiting on me or some deadline I’m trying to keep.

And it’s frustrating because part of me knows I don’t have to be doing all of it right then. I’ll think, “Just sit down for a while,” but then I see one thing that needs fixing or picking up or checking, and then I’m off doing that. Then that turns into something else. By the end of the day I’ve been busy all day, but I don’t always feel settled or satisfied — more like I’ve been chased around by tasks.

So yes, overwhelmed might be the right word sometimes. It’s not that the tasks themselves are always huge, it’s the constant pull to keep moving that gets tiring.
Do you feel like your inability to slow down and constant need to do tasks is significantly affecting your relationships with your family and friends?

Yes, it is affecting them, especially at home. My wife has kind of become the person who keeps the whole calendar straight for us. If there’s an appointment, or something with friends, or something we agreed to do, she’s usually the one tracking it and reminding me. And sometimes she checks behind me, too, which I don’t blame her for, but it doesn’t feel good. It makes me feel like she has to manage me instead of just being my wife.

And outside the family, with the community center and the garden group, I’ve had to apologize more than once because I said I’d do something or be somewhere and then I let people down. I don’t mean to. I’ll get caught up doing one thing after another, and the thing I promised just slips or doesn’t get done right. Then I feel embarrassed, because these are people I like and I want them to be able to count on me.

So yes, I wouldn’t say it’s ruining every relationship or anything like that, but it’s definitely causing strain. People have to compensate for me, and I can tell that’s not fair to them.
Are there any areas of your life where you feel like you're not functioning as well as you used to because of your constant need to be active and do tasks?

Yes, I’d say so. The main place I notice it is with keeping track of things and following through, especially now that I don’t have work giving me a structure every day.

My wife has really had to take over the calendar for us — appointments, plans with people, things we said we’d do. She’ll remind me, and sometimes she’ll check behind me to make sure I actually did what I said I was going to do. I don’t love admitting that, because it makes me feel like I’m not holding up my end as well as I should.

And then with things like the community center and the garden group, I’ve had to apologize more than once because I let people down. I’ll mean well, I’ll agree to something, and then I get pulled into one task after another and I don’t follow through the way I used to. It’s embarrassing, honestly. It’s not that I don’t care — I do care — but I’m not functioning as reliably as I’d like in those parts of my life.
Are you feeling like your inability to slow down and constant need to do tasks is making it hard for you to enjoy leisure activities or relax?

Yes, it does. That’s actually one of the parts that bothers me, because I used to think of relaxing as, you know, sitting down with a book or doing a little sketching, something quiet like that. And now I don’t seem to stay with those things very well for long.

I’ll sit down to read, and at first I’m trying to enjoy it, but then I notice I’m humming, or I’m talking under my breath to myself about something I just thought of. Or I’ll get up because I remembered some little thing I wanted to adjust or check, and then I’m not reading anymore. Same with sketching — I’ll start, and then before too long I’m shifting around, making noises, getting up to mess with something nearby.

It’s not that I don’t want to relax. I do. I just don’t seem to settle into quiet activities the way I’d like to. It feels like even when I’m trying to be still, part of me is still looking for something to do.
Do you feel like your constant need to be active and do tasks is causing you significant distress or problems in your daily life?

Yes, I’d say it’s causing problems, even if I keep wanting to tell myself it’s “not that bad.” The biggest daily-life thing is that my wife has had to sort of take over keeping the calendar for us. She tracks appointments, plans, things we told people we’d do, and then she’ll remind me or check behind me to make sure I actually followed through.

And I understand why she does it, I really do, but it bothers me. It makes me feel like I’m creating extra work for her, like she has to supervise me in a way she shouldn’t have to. That’s distressing.

Then outside the house, I’ve had to apologize more than once to people at the community center and the garden group because I said I’d do something and then didn’t come through. I hate that feeling — letting people down when I didn’t mean to. So yes, it’s not destroying my life, but it is definitely causing strain and making parts of everyday life harder than they should be.

Are you finding that your difficulty in slowing down and constant need to do tasks is significantly impairing your ability to function in your daily life, such as in your relationships, work, or other activities?

Yes, I think it is impairing things, mostly in the day-to-day responsibilities and with people depending on me.

At home, my wife has really had to take over the calendar. She keeps track of appointments, plans, and things we’ve committed to, and then she’ll remind me or even check behind me to make sure I actually did what I said I was going to do. I don’t like that, because it makes me feel like she has to manage me, almost, and that’s not fair to her.

And outside the house, it’s shown up with the community center and the garden group. I’ll agree to help with something, and I really do intend to follow through, but then I don’t, and I’ve had to apologize more than once for letting people down. That’s embarrassing. So yes, it’s not like I can’t function at all, but it’s definitely affecting my relationships and the activities I’m involved in.

I don’t know that I’d call it anxious exactly, or unhappy in the way you might mean. It’s more like I get… unsettled, I guess. Like if I’m not moving from one thing to the next, something feels off, like I’m wasting time or I’m supposed to be doing something.

Since I stopped working, that’s been the strange part. I thought I’d slow down, but I don’t. There’s no crew waiting on me anymore, nobody asking me to get anything done, but my body acts like there is.

So if I try to just sit there, I don’t always feel bad exactly, but I don’t stay there long. I start looking around, noticing something that could be fixed or cleaned or moved, and then I’m back up again. It’s like I don’t know how to just stop.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say I repeat the same thing over and over in a set way. Not like I have to touch something a certain number of times or keep checking the same lock or anything like that — at least, I haven’t really noticed that.

I do circle back to things sometimes, but it feels more like I forgot where I left off or I notice something again and think, “Oh, I should deal with that,” not like a ritual. Like I might tidy an area, then later see another thing out of place and end up back over there, but it’s not the exact same behavior in my mind.

So… I guess no, not repeating in a particular pattern. More just moving around and getting pulled into things as they come up.
